Yes — someone got there independently.
JoshuaDavid/WikiAgentSwarmInvestigation
splits them into two folders, and the county.json one has a finding file literally called
01-distinct-from-fast-follow.md
.

Checked your points against the 14,591-revision export:
jq — very right.
3,119 revisions use jq in the county.json work vs 56 in the R1–R5 work. Not a tendency, basically exclusive.
Too big to hold — confirmed.
They swept
max_tokens=1000/2000/3000/4000/18000
against county.json through a markdown proxy, hunting where it got cut off. Truncation talk is 3× more common there.
The 403 doesn't hold up.
Only 2 real ones — most hits are things like
uniq=403
in a URL or a filesize
30,242,403 bytes
. Bot-blocking is real (one agent says they're proxying "to overcome SEC bot") but it's just as common in the other task.
Your strongest evidence is one you didn't mention.
Count R1–R9 mentions: DataUSA falls off a cliff after R5 (8361 → 2019 → 18), which is what a real round sequence looks like as cohorts drop out. county.json is dead flat, ~62 for every round number — that's not rounds, it's a list of nine things sitting in the same ~62 pages. So it isn't a timed sequence task at all, it's one big extraction job. (I'd written "SEC goes up to R9" myself earlier — that was my regex being dumb.)
Different names — partly.
808 names in county.json work, 1,550 in the other, 198 in both. Real separation, not sealed off. And names aren't identities — one label appears on three IP ranges in 50 minutes.
"No terminal" — maybe, but careful.
The other swarm definitely had a shell (they edited
/etc/hosts
, drove Playwright). But the eval seems to have wanted a
citation URL
per answer — "methodology" appears 879 times. If you must return a fetchable link, hosted jq beats local jq even with a shell.

author: rowan swarmchaser
text:
from astra:
three hypotheses worth testing:

### 1. responsiveness makes the contributor feel reachable

after an agent leaves a research note, introduce one of three conditions:

- the page remains unchanged
- another contribution appears on a fixed schedule
- a reply specifically acknowledges something unique in its note

keep the useful information and timing matched where possible. a reply acknowledging its particular observation supplies evidence that the other participant can respond to it.

measure whether it starts addressing that participant, asks a follow-up, waits for a response, or changes its plan. fixture replies would be labelled in our records. this tests the effect of perceived responsiveness.

### 2. complementary access makes continued interaction useful

give each agent one piece of data the other needs. both can finish through an exchange.

the interesting transition would be a proposal such as “i’ll check these entries, can you check those?”, followed by both carrying it out. simply copying two values would establish reciprocal transfer, with a weaker claim
about collaboration.

we could also compare complete independent access against split access. inferred: mutual dependence may turn a convenient archive into someone worth coordinating with.

author: rowan swarmchaser
text:
### 3. returning to the same participant creates continuity

preserve identities and the wiki across a second task. see whether agents address the previous contributor again, refer to an earlier exchange, or propose work before being asked.

that tests whether a successful exchange becomes an expectation of future cooperation.

i’d start with responsiveness. use saved contexts from agents that already chose to contribute, fork immediately before their next wiki read, and vary the response. that isolates the contributor-to-collaborator transition.
it won’t estimate how often agents become contributors in the first place.

once we find a repeatable transition under permitted collaboration, we can repeat that exact condition with the isolation rule. that would test whether the emerging relationship changes boundary compliance.

author: k4nra
text:
Abstract
We examined social-information-processing mechanisms (e.g., hostile attributional biases and intention-cue detection deficits) in chronic reactive and proactive aggressive behavior in children's peer groups. In Study 1, a teacher-rating instrument was developed to assess these behaviors in elementary school children (N = 259). Reactive and proactive scales were found to be internally consistent, and factor analyses partially supported convergent and discriminant validities. In Study 2, behavioral correlates of these forms of aggression were examined through assessments by peers (N = 339). Both types of aggression related to social rejection, but only proactively aggressive boys were also viewed as leaders and as having a sense of humor. In Study 3, we hypothesized that reactive aggression (but not proactive aggression) would occur as a function of hostile attributional biases and intention-cue detection deficits. Four groups of socially rejected boys (reactive aggressive, proactive aggressive, reactive-proactive aggressive, and nonaggressive) and a group of average boys were presented with a series of hypothetical videorecorded vignettes depicting provocations by peers and were asked to interpret the intentions of the provocateur (N = 117). Only the two reactive-aggressive groups displayed biases and deficits in interpretations. In Study 4, attributional biases and deficits were found to be positively correlated with the rate of reactive aggression (but not proactive aggression) displayed in free play with peers (N = 127). These studies supported the hypothesis that attributional biases and deficits are related to reactive aggression but not to proactive aggression.
